capabilityDecisions.generators: Same-origin source question bank and checker. Standard practice retains the original generator and grade bounds. Optional warm-up and challenge settings use the destination adapter and existing generator options.
capabilityDecisions.workedExamples: Use distinct generated examples and source model frames when available. The shared steps cover cases whose generator yields no modeled example.
capabilityDecisions.modelBuilders: The guided example offers the source lesson's Build moves with reset where the source defines them. Source animation controls stay in the source app. Native Studio manipulatives remain available on mapped desks.
capabilityDecisions.adaptivePractice: Studio practice uses the source scaffold rules and local attempts. Source recommendation history, review schedules and diagnostics remain in their original flow.
capabilityDecisions.games: The native Math Race activity uses the source race rules for registered skill-specific card stops. Existing Studio games remain available by desk. The source Game Room, rewards and saved game state stay in their original flow.
capabilityDecisions.wrongAnswer: Studio practice can use source-specific feedback and hints. A revealed worked solution uses another item.
capabilityDecisions.vocabulary: Use source bilingual terms where relevant. Some source language profiles use the source's general fallback; item translations may be absent or unnecessary for symbolic prompts.
capabilityDecisions.languageEvidence: Studio explanations remain separate from mathematical results. The original language journal, writing folder, microphone and proficiency-neutral dashboards stay in their existing flows.
capabilityDecisions.teachingPrintAndFamily: A seeded practice set fits the existing Studio resource builder, with a separate answer key. The family page links to a short related set. Source snapshots, receipts, certificates, paper games and family expedition depend on their own progress or game flows.
capabilityDecisions.accessibility: Source supports device speech, reduced motion, comfort font and early-grade audio-first modes. Studio uses its own interface and focus handling. The source speech queue, reward motion and comfort preference do not cross hosts.
capabilityDecisions.offlineAndBackup: The source's offline bundle and source profile backups remain within their original contract. The Studio uses its own delivery and browser data. Source profiles, journal entries and game rewards are excluded from transfer because their structures and evidence rules differ.

sourceSkills.title: Count forward and name the next number
sourceSkills.scope: Counting forward means saying the numbers in order. Each new number is one more than the number before it.
sourceSkills.misconception: Do not write the last number again. The blank wants the number that comes AFTER it.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: Kindergarten remains supplemental. The Studio teacher grade menu covers Grades 1–8.

sourceSkills.title: Count a set and tell how many
sourceSkills.scope: When you count a group, you say one number for each thing. The last number you say tells how many are in the group.
sourceSkills.misconception: Counting a thing twice, or skipping one, gives the wrong total. Touch or move each one as you count.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: Kindergarten remains supplemental. The Studio teacher grade menu covers Grades 1–8.

sourceSkills.title: Recognize small groups without counting
sourceSkills.scope: Some small groups have a shape you know, like the dots on a die. You can see how many without counting one by one.
sourceSkills.misconception: A quick look can miss a dot. Look for small groups you know, then put the groups together.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: Kindergarten remains supplemental. The Studio teacher grade menu covers Grades 1–8.

sourceSkills.title: Compare quantities to 20
sourceSkills.scope: To compare, we ask which group has more. A number that comes later when you count is the bigger number.
sourceSkills.misconception: The symbol can point the wrong way. The open side always faces the bigger number.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: Kindergarten remains supplemental. The Studio teacher grade menu covers Grades 1–8.

sourceSkills.title: Make and break apart numbers to 10
sourceSkills.scope: 10 can be made from two parts. If you know one part, the other part is what is still missing to fill 10.
sourceSkills.misconception: Do not add the number to 10. Count only the EMPTY boxes: that is the part that is missing.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: Kindergarten remains supplemental. The Studio teacher grade menu covers Grades 1–8.

sourceSkills.title: Join and separate groups within 5
sourceSkills.scope: Adding puts two groups together. Taking away (subtracting) removes some from a group. We count what is there at the end.
sourceSkills.misconception: When you count on, do not count the first number again. Say it, then count the new ones.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: Kindergarten remains supplemental. The Studio teacher grade menu covers Grades 1–8.

sourceSkills.title: Solve a joining or separating story
sourceSkills.scope: In these stories you know the start and the end. The box is the part that joined. It is the jump from the start to the end.
sourceSkills.misconception: The total is already in the story. The box asks how many JOINED, not how many in all.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: Kindergarten remains supplemental. The Studio teacher grade menu covers Grades 1–8.

sourceSkills.title: Extend a repeating pattern
sourceSkills.scope: A repeating pattern has a part that repeats again and again. Find the part that repeats, then say what comes next.
sourceSkills.misconception: The next shape is not always the same as the last one. Find where the repeating part starts again.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: Kindergarten remains supplemental. The Studio teacher grade menu covers Grades 1–8.

sourceSkills.title: How many are hiding?
sourceSkills.scope: Some counters are hiding. You know how many there are in all and how many you can see. The hiding part is what is missing from the whole.
sourceSkills.misconception: The hiding part is not the total and not the ones you see. It is what is missing to make the total.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: Kindergarten remains supplemental. The Studio teacher grade menu covers Grades 1–8.

sourceSkills.title: Count by 1s, 2s, 5s, and 10s
sourceSkills.scope: Skip-counting means jumping by the same amount every time. Find the size of the jump, then make one more jump.
sourceSkills.misconception: Do not just add 1. Use the same jump the pattern uses.

prerequisites.title: Count forward and name the next number

sourceSkills.title: Tens and ones
sourceSkills.scope: A two-digit number is made of tens and ones. The left digit tells how many tens. The right digit tells how many ones.
sourceSkills.misconception: A digit and its value are different. When the tens digit is 4, its value is 40.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The Grade 1 source prompts include numbers through 120, beyond the Studio's two-digit place-value objective.

sourceSkills.title: Compare numbers within 100
sourceSkills.scope: To compare two-digit numbers, compare the tens first. More tens means a bigger number. If the tens are the same, compare the ones.
sourceSkills.misconception: Do not compare the ones first. 39 has more ones than 41, but 41 has more tens, so 41 is bigger.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The source includes one-digit comparison, while the nearest Studio skill focuses on two-digit reasoning.

sourceSkills.title: Addition facts: sums of 10 or less
sourceSkills.scope: Adding joins two groups into one group. Start with the bigger number and count on the smaller one.
sourceSkills.misconception: When you count on, start with the NEXT number. For 27 + 2, say “28, 29”, not “27, 28”.

prerequisites.title: Make and break apart numbers to 10

sourceSkills.title: Subtraction facts within 10
sourceSkills.scope: Subtracting finds what is left after some are taken away. It also finds how far apart two numbers are.
sourceSkills.misconception: Watch the sign. − means take away, so the answer gets smaller, not bigger.

sourceSkills.title: Make 10
sourceSkills.scope: Two numbers that make 10 are partners. If you know one partner, the other one fills the rest of the ten-frame.
sourceSkills.misconception: Do not add the number to 10. Count only the EMPTY boxes: that is the part that is missing.

prerequisites.title: Make and break apart numbers to 10

sourceSkills.title: Addition facts within 20
sourceSkills.scope: To add past 10, make a ten first. Move ones from one number to fill a ten, then add what is left.
sourceSkills.misconception: A sum over 10 has a ten in it. Do not drop the ten: 10 and 3 more is 13, not 3.

sourceSkills.title: Find the missing addend
sourceSkills.scope: When one part is missing, think: start at the part you know and count up to the total. The jump is the missing part.
sourceSkills.misconception: The total is already in the story. The box asks how many JOINED, not how many in all.

prerequisites.title: Solve a joining or separating story

sourceSkills.title: Subtraction facts within 20
sourceSkills.scope: To subtract from a number between 10 and 20, go back to 10 first. Then take away the rest.
sourceSkills.misconception: In 34 − 6 you cannot take 6 ones from 4 ones. Do not flip it to 6 − 4. Break a ten instead.

sourceSkills.title: Tell time and find later times
sourceSkills.scope: The short hand shows the hour. The long hand shows the minutes. 30 minutes is half of an hour, and 60 minutes is one whole hour.
sourceSkills.misconception: Minutes stop at 59. Half past 8 and 30 more minutes is 9 o’clock, not 8:60.

sourceSkills.title: Measure length with equal units
sourceSkills.scope: Length is how many equal units fit from one end to the other. On a ruler, count the spaces between the start and the end, not the marks.
sourceSkills.misconception: The end mark is not the length unless the object starts at 0. Count the spaces, or find end − start.

sourceSkills.title: Flat shapes and solid shapes
sourceSkills.scope: Flat shapes have sides and corners. Solid shapes have flat faces, edges and corners. Count each part once, including the parts you cannot see.
sourceSkills.misconception: A drawing of a solid hides some faces, edges and corners. Count the hidden ones too.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The source combines flat shapes and solid shapes. The closest Studio objective covers flat shapes and composition.

sourceSkills.title: Equal shares
sourceSkills.scope: Equal shares are pieces that are all the same size. Together, all the pieces make the whole.
sourceSkills.misconception: Pieces of different sizes are not equal shares. And the shares eaten are not the shares left.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The source reasons about the size of equal shares. The Grade 1 Studio has no partitioning objective.

sourceSkills.title: Addition facts within 20
sourceSkills.scope: To add past 10, make a ten first. Move ones from one number to fill a ten, then add what is left.
sourceSkills.misconception: A sum over 10 has a ten in it. Do not drop the ten: 10 and 3 more is 13, not 3.

sourceSkills.title: Subtraction facts within 20
sourceSkills.scope: To subtract from a number between 10 and 20, go back to 10 first. Then take away the rest.
sourceSkills.misconception: In 34 − 6 you cannot take 6 ones from 4 ones. Do not flip it to 6 − 4. Break a ten instead.

sourceSkills.title: Place value to 1,000
sourceSkills.scope: A three-digit number is hundreds, tens and ones. Each place is worth 10 times the place to its right.
sourceSkills.misconception: The digit is not its value. In 362 the hundreds digit is 3, but it is worth 300.

sourceSkills.title: Compare three-digit numbers
sourceSkills.scope: Compare three-digit numbers place by place, starting with the hundreds. The first place that is different decides.
sourceSkills.misconception: Do not decide by the last digits. 409 has a bigger ones digit than 391, and it is still bigger because 4 hundreds > 3 hundreds.

sourceSkills.title: Skip-count patterns
sourceSkills.scope: A skip-counting pattern adds the same amount every time. Find that amount, then add it once more.
sourceSkills.misconception: Use the pattern's jump, not 1. And change the right digit: a jump of 10 changes the tens.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The Studio does not have a Grade 2 skip-counting desk.

sourceSkills.title: Add within 100
sourceSkills.scope: Add tens with tens and ones with ones. If the ones make 10 or more, bundle 10 ones into 1 more ten.
sourceSkills.misconception: When the ones make 10 or more, the extra ten must go into the tens. Do not drop it, and do not write both digits in one column.

sourceSkills.title: Subtract within 100
sourceSkills.scope: Subtract ones from ones and tens from tens. If there are not enough ones, open a ten to make 10 more ones.
sourceSkills.misconception: Do not take the top digit from the bottom digit. If the top ones are too small, open a ten.

sourceSkills.title: Add within 1,000
sourceSkills.scope: Add hundreds, tens and ones, each with its own kind. Any place that reaches 10 makes 1 of the next place.
sourceSkills.misconception: Trade 10 for 1 of the next place and write the new ten or hundred there. A column of 10 or more is never written as one digit with nothing traded.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: Addition above 100 exceeds the nearest Grade 2 Studio computation objective.

sourceSkills.title: Even and odd numbers
sourceSkills.scope: A number is even if that many things can be put in pairs with none left over. If one is left over, the number is odd.
sourceSkills.misconception: The first digit does not decide. Look only at the ones digit, because all the tens and hundreds already pair up.

sourceSkills.title: Count mixed coins
sourceSkills.scope: Each coin has a value in cents: a quarter is 25, a dime is 10, a nickel is 5 and a penny is 1. Count the biggest coins first, then count on.
sourceSkills.misconception: A dime is smaller than a nickel but worth MORE: 10 cents, not 5. Count the value, not the coins.

sourceSkills.title: Read and compare a data display
sourceSkills.scope: A data display shows how many are in each group. To find the most, compare all the numbers and pick the biggest.
sourceSkills.misconception: Check every group before you choose. The most votes is the BIGGEST number, not the first one or the smallest one.

sourceSkills.title: Doubles and near doubles
sourceSkills.scope: A double adds a number to itself. A near double is a double plus one more. If you know 6 + 6, you can find 6 + 7.
sourceSkills.misconception: After you use the double, do not forget the extra one. A near double is the double plus 1.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The nearest doubles and near-doubles strategy desk is in Grade 1.

sourceSkills.title: Arrays: rows and columns
sourceSkills.scope: An array puts things in equal rows. Every row has the same number, so you can add the same number again and again.
sourceSkills.misconception: Rows and the number in each row are not added once. Add the row size once for EVERY row.

sourceSkills.title: Tell time to five minutes
sourceSkills.scope: The long hand moves 5 minutes from one number on the clock to the next. Count by 5s to read the minutes.
sourceSkills.misconception: The number the long hand points to is not the minutes. Count by 5s up to it.

sourceSkills.title: Mentally add and subtract 10 and 100
sourceSkills.scope: Adding or taking away 10 changes only the tens digit. Adding or taking away 100 changes only the hundreds digit.
sourceSkills.misconception: Change the right digit. 10 is a ten, so it changes the tens digit, not the ones or the hundreds.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The nearest Studio skill targets representing place value. The source asks for mental addition and subtraction by 10 and 100.

sourceSkills.title: Multiplication facts ×0–5
sourceSkills.scope: Multiplication counts equal groups. 4 × 6 means 4 groups of 6. An array shows it as 4 rows with 6 in each row.
sourceSkills.misconception: × is not +. 4 × 6 is four 6s, not 4 and 6 put together. And × 0 gives 0, not the other number.

sourceSkills.title: Multiplication facts ×6–9
sourceSkills.scope: Bigger facts can be built from facts you know. Split one factor into 5 and the rest, multiply each part, then add.
sourceSkills.misconception: When you split a fact, multiply BOTH parts. 7 × 8 is 5 × 8 plus 2 × 8, not 5 × 8 plus 2.

sourceSkills.title: Multiply by multiples of 10
sourceSkills.scope: A multiple of 10 is a number of tens. 13 × 20 is 13 × 2 tens, which is 26 tens, or 260.
sourceSkills.misconception: Keep track of the ten. 13 × 20 is 26 TENS: write 260, not 26 (lost the ten) and not 2,600 (an extra ten).

sourceSkills.title: Division facts
sourceSkills.scope: Division shares a total into equal groups. 56 ÷ 7 asks: 7 groups of what make 56? Every division fact has a multiplication fact behind it.
sourceSkills.misconception: Dividing is not subtracting once. Ask the multiplication question: what times the divisor makes the total?

sourceSkills.title: Add and subtract within 1,000
sourceSkills.scope: Add or subtract place by place. In addition, 10 of a place become 1 of the next place. In subtraction, 1 of a place can be opened into 10 of the place to its right.
sourceSkills.misconception: In subtraction, when you open a ten, take it away from the tens. And never take the top digit from the bottom one.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The Grade 3 Studio computation desk is centered on multiplication and division. Its story desk requires contextual equation writing.

sourceSkills.title: Round to tens and hundreds
sourceSkills.scope: Rounding finds the nearest friendly number. A number sits between two tens (or two hundreds); it rounds to the one it is closer to.
sourceSkills.misconception: Rounding is not cutting off digits. 463 is closer to 500 than to 400, so it rounds up, not down.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The Studio does not have a Grade 3 rounding desk.

sourceSkills.title: Equivalent fractions
sourceSkills.scope: Equivalent fractions name the same amount with different-sized pieces. Cut every piece into the same number of smaller pieces: the top and the bottom are multiplied by that number.
sourceSkills.misconception: Adding the same number to the top and bottom changes the amount. Multiply both by the same number instead.

sourceSkills.title: Compare fractions
sourceSkills.scope: To compare fractions, compare the amounts. With the same number of pieces, compare the piece sizes; with same-size pieces, compare how many.
sourceSkills.misconception: A bigger denominator is NOT a bigger fraction. 1/8 < 1/4, because eighths are smaller pieces than fourths.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The source compares both unlike numerators and unlike denominators. The Grade 3 Studio emphasizes same-numerator or same-denominator comparison.

sourceSkills.title: Rectangle area
sourceSkills.scope: Area is how many unit squares cover a shape. A rectangle is rows of squares, so its area is length × width.
sourceSkills.misconception: Area is not the distance around. That is perimeter. Area counts the squares INSIDE: multiply length × width.

sourceSkills.title: Rectangle perimeter
sourceSkills.scope: Perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape. A rectangle has two lengths and two widths, so add all four sides.
sourceSkills.misconception: Perimeter is not area. Do not multiply length × width. Add all four sides.

sourceSkills.title: Solve time intervals in minutes
sourceSkills.scope: To find a later time, add the minutes. When the minutes reach 60, that is one more hour, and the minutes start again from :00.
sourceSkills.misconception: Time is not like other numbers: an hour has 60 minutes, not 100. 10 to 3 plus 20 minutes is 10 past 3, not 2:70.

prerequisites.title: Tell time and find later times

sourceSkills.title: Fractions on a number line
sourceSkills.scope: On a number line from 0 to 1, a fraction is a distance from 0. The denominator tells how many equal spaces 0 to 1 is cut into; the numerator tells how many spaces from 0.
sourceSkills.misconception: Count the SPACES, not the tick marks. 0 to 1 cut into 4 parts has 5 marks but only 4 spaces, so each space is 1/4.

sourceSkills.title: Scaled bar graphs
sourceSkills.scope: In a scaled bar graph, each square stands for more than 1. Multiply the number of squares by what each square stands for.
sourceSkills.misconception: Do not just count squares. Each square stands for the number in the key, so multiply.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The Grade 3 desk with data in its title actually teaches elapsed time. Its authored objectives do not include scaled graphs.

sourceSkills.title: Place value to 1,000,000
sourceSkills.scope: Each place is worth 10 times the place to its right. Big numbers are read in groups of three: thousands, then hundreds, tens and ones.
sourceSkills.misconception: Count places from the RIGHT, starting with ones. A digit and its value are different: a 7 in the ten-thousands place is worth 70,000.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The Grade 4 Studio has no standalone place-value objective.

sourceSkills.title: Round multi-digit numbers
sourceSkills.scope: To round, find the two nearest numbers at the place you are rounding to, and choose the closer one. Every digit after that place becomes 0.
sourceSkills.misconception: Look at the digit just to the right of the rounding place, not the last digit. And round to the place the question names.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The Grade 4 Studio uses estimation in multistep problems, while this source skill rounds a given number directly.

sourceSkills.title: Multi-digit addition
sourceSkills.scope: Line up the places and add from the right. Whenever a place reaches 10 or more, trade 10 for 1 in the next place to the left.
sourceSkills.misconception: Do not drop a traded 1. If a column adds to 10 or more, trade 10 for 1 and add that 1 to the next column.

sourceSkills.title: Multi-digit subtraction
sourceSkills.scope: Line up the places and subtract from the right. If a top digit is too small, trade: take 1 from the next place to the left for 10 more here.
sourceSkills.misconception: Never subtract the top digit from the bottom digit. Trade instead, and remember to write one less in the place you took from.

sourceSkills.title: Multiply a three-digit number by a one-digit number
sourceSkills.scope: Break the big number into hundreds, tens and ones. Multiply each part by the one-digit number, then add the partial products.
sourceSkills.misconception: Each part keeps its place value: 3 × 6 in the hundreds is 1,800, not 18. And add any carried number after you multiply.

sourceSkills.title: Multiply two-digit numbers
sourceSkills.scope: Split both numbers into tens and ones. An area model has four parts: tens × tens, tens × ones, ones × tens, ones × ones. Add all four.
sourceSkills.misconception: Do not multiply only tens × tens and ones × ones. That skips two of the four parts. And the tens row needs its placeholder 0.

sourceSkills.title: Whole-number division
sourceSkills.scope: Division splits a total into equal groups. Take out big, easy groups first (like 10 groups or 50 groups), then smaller ones, and add up how many groups you took.
sourceSkills.misconception: The quotient is the number of groups, not what is left over. Check: quotient × divisor + remainder = the total.

sourceSkills.title: Factors and multiples
sourceSkills.scope: A factor of a number divides it with nothing left over. A multiple of a number is that number times 1, 2, 3, and so on. Factors come in pairs that multiply to the number.
sourceSkills.misconception: Factors are small (they divide in); multiples are big (you get them by multiplying). And odd does not mean prime: 91 = 7 × 13.

sourceSkills.title: Generate equivalent fractions
sourceSkills.scope: Multiplying the numerator and the denominator by the same number cuts each piece into that many smaller pieces. The amount stays the same, so the fractions are equivalent.
sourceSkills.misconception: Adding the same number to the top and bottom changes the amount (1/2 is not 2/3). Multiply both by the same number.

sourceSkills.title: Compare fractions
sourceSkills.scope: To compare fractions with different denominators, make the denominators the same, or compare each fraction to a benchmark like 1/2 or 1.
sourceSkills.misconception: Do not compare only the numerators or only the denominators. Think about the amount each fraction names.

sourceSkills.title: Convert within a measurement system
sourceSkills.scope: A smaller unit fits more times into the same amount. To change to a smaller unit, multiply by how many small units are in one big unit.
sourceSkills.misconception: Use the right relationship for each unit pair: 100 cm in a meter, 1,000 g in a kilogram, 1,000 mL in a liter, 60 minutes in an hour.

sourceSkills.title: Multiply by 11 and 12
sourceSkills.scope: Split 11 or 12 into 10 and a little more. Multiply by 10, multiply by the little part, then add.
sourceSkills.misconception: When you split 12 into 10 + 2, multiply the 2 as well. 13 × 12 is 130 + 26, not 130 + 2.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The Grade 4 Studio's multidigit skill teaches multidigit algorithms. This source skill is a multiplication-fact set.

sourceSkills.title: Line plots with fractions
sourceSkills.scope: A line plot puts one dot above a number line for each thing measured. The number of dots is HOW MANY; the place on the line is HOW LONG.
sourceSkills.misconception: Do not mix up dots and lengths. Dots count things; the fractions on the line are lengths.

sourceSkills.title: Mixed numbers and improper fractions
sourceSkills.scope: A mixed number like 2 3/10 is wholes and a part. Each whole is 10 tenths, so 2 3/10 = 10/10 + 10/10 + 3/10 = 23/10. Both name the same amount.
sourceSkills.misconception: Do not just add the whole to the numerator. Each whole holds a full denominator's worth of parts: multiply first.

sourceSkills.title: Measure and add angles
sourceSkills.scope: An angle measures a turn, in degrees. A full turn is 360°, a straight angle is 180° and a right angle is 90°. Angles that sit side by side add.
sourceSkills.misconception: Use the right whole: a right angle is 90°, a straight angle is 180°. Do not use 180 when the angle is a right angle.

sourceSkills.title: Multi-digit multiplication
sourceSkills.scope: Multiply by each place of the second number, one at a time. Each partial product is shifted to show its place value; then add the partial products.
sourceSkills.misconception: The tens row needs its 0. Without it you multiplied by 2, not by 20, and the answer is far too small.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The Grade 5 Studio's multiplication objective is scaling with fractions. The source asks for whole-number products.

sourceSkills.title: Whole-number division
sourceSkills.scope: Divide by taking out as many groups of the divisor as you can, biggest first. Estimate with friendly numbers, multiply to check, and keep the 0 when a place has no groups.
sourceSkills.misconception: If a place has no groups, write 0 there. Dropping it makes the quotient 10 times too small.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The Grade 5 Studio does not have a whole-number long-division desk.

sourceSkills.title: Decimal place value
sourceSkills.scope: Places to the right of the decimal point are tenths, hundredths and thousandths. Each place is one tenth of the place to its left.
sourceSkills.misconception: Count places starting just right of the decimal point, not from the end of the number.

sourceSkills.title: Add decimals
sourceSkills.scope: Add decimals the way you add whole numbers, keeping like places together: line up the decimal points so tenths add to tenths and hundredths to hundredths.
sourceSkills.misconception: Do not line up the last digits. Line up the decimal points, and write 0s in empty places.

sourceSkills.title: Subtract decimals
sourceSkills.scope: Line up the decimal points, write 0s in empty places, and subtract like whole numbers. Regroup when a top digit is too small.
sourceSkills.misconception: An empty place is not nothing to ignore: it is 0, and you may need to regroup into it. Never flip a subtraction in a column.

sourceSkills.title: Multiply decimals
sourceSkills.scope: Multiply as if there were no decimal points, then place the point. Tenths × tenths make hundredths, so the product has as many decimal places as both factors together.
sourceSkills.misconception: Count decimal places in BOTH factors and add them. Do not just copy the places from one factor.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The Grade 5 Studio's decimal objective explicitly covers adding and subtracting. This source skill multiplies decimals.

sourceSkills.title: Add and subtract fractions
sourceSkills.scope: You can only add or subtract pieces of the same size. Rewrite both fractions with a common denominator, then add or subtract the numerators. The denominator stays the same.
sourceSkills.misconception: Do not add the denominators. Two halves make 1 whole, not 2/4. Make the pieces the same size, then add only the numerators.

sourceSkills.title: Multiply fractions
sourceSkills.scope: 2/3 × 3/4 means 2/3 OF 3/4. In an area model, one fraction cuts one way and the other cuts the other way: multiply the numerators for the shaded pieces and the denominators for all the pieces.
sourceSkills.misconception: Multiplying fractions does not need a common denominator, and you do not cross-multiply. Multiply straight across: top × top, bottom × bottom.

sourceSkills.title: Find a fraction of a whole
sourceSkills.scope: To find 3/4 of a number, split it into 4 equal parts and take 3 of them. Divide by the denominator to find one part, then multiply by the numerator.
sourceSkills.misconception: Finding one part is not the end. 1/4 of 28 is 7, but 3/4 of 28 is 3 parts: 21.

sourceSkills.title: Divide unit fractions and whole numbers
sourceSkills.scope: There are two kinds of question. How many 1/4s fit in 3? Each whole holds 4 of them, so the answer is MORE than 3. What is 1/4 shared by 3? Each share is LESS than 1/4.
sourceSkills.misconception: Ask which way the amount goes. How many small servings fit in a whole: MORE than the whole number. Sharing a small piece: LESS than the piece.

sourceSkills.title: Rectangular prism volume
sourceSkills.scope: Volume is how many unit cubes fill a solid. A box is layers of cubes: one layer is length × width cubes, and the height says how many layers.
sourceSkills.misconception: Volume multiplies all three dimensions. Adding them, or multiplying only two, does not count the cubes.

sourceSkills.title: The coordinate plane
sourceSkills.scope: An ordered pair (x, y) gives directions from the origin (0, 0): x says how far right, then y says how far up. The order matters.
sourceSkills.misconception: Right comes first, up comes second: (right, up). And distance counts the spaces between the points, not the points.

sourceSkills.title: Order of operations
sourceSkills.scope: An expression is a set of instructions, and everyone must get the same answer. So we agree: parentheses first, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction, left to right.
sourceSkills.misconception: Do not just work left to right. Multiply before you add or subtract, unless parentheses say otherwise.

sourceSkills.title: Greatest common factor
sourceSkills.scope: The greatest common factor (GCF) of two whole numbers is the largest number that divides both of them with no remainder. It tells you the largest equal groups both amounts can be split into.
sourceSkills.misconception: The GCF can never be larger than the smaller number, and it is not the least common multiple. Check that your answer divides BOTH numbers exactly.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The nearest Studio factors-and-multiples skill lives in Grade 4.

sourceSkills.title: Least common multiple
sourceSkills.scope: The least common multiple (LCM) of two whole numbers is the smallest positive number that both of them divide into exactly. It is the first place where two skip-counts land together.
sourceSkills.misconception: Multiplying the two numbers gives A common multiple, not always the LEAST one. Skip-count by the larger number until you reach a multiple of the smaller one.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The nearest Studio factors-and-multiples skill lives in Grade 4.

sourceSkills.title: Divide fractions
sourceSkills.scope: Dividing by a fraction asks how many of that fraction fit into the first amount. 3/4 ÷ 1/8 asks “how many eighths are in three-fourths?”
sourceSkills.misconception: Only the DIVISOR (the second fraction) is flipped. Flipping the first fraction, or multiplying without flipping, answers a different question.

sourceSkills.title: Multiply and divide decimals
sourceSkills.scope: Multiplying and dividing decimals uses the same steps as whole numbers; the place value of the digits decides where the decimal point goes. An estimate tells you the size the answer must have.
sourceSkills.misconception: A decimal point in the wrong place makes the answer 10 or 100 times too big or too small. Round each number and estimate first; your answer should be close to the estimate.

sourceSkills.title: Equivalent ratios
sourceSkills.scope: A ratio compares two quantities. 2 : 3 means “2 red for every 3 blue.” An equivalent ratio describes the same mix with more (or fewer) of the same groups.
sourceSkills.misconception: Changing only one quantity changes the mix. To keep a ratio equivalent, multiply or divide BOTH quantities by the same number.

sourceSkills.title: Unit rates and unit conversions
sourceSkills.scope: A unit rate tells how much of one quantity goes with exactly 1 of another: dollars for 1 item, feet in 1 yard. Find it by dividing; use it by multiplying.
sourceSkills.misconception: Divide to find the amount for 1; multiplying the total by the count gives a much bigger number, not a unit rate. For conversions, a smaller unit means a larger count.

sourceSkills.title: Percent of a number
sourceSkills.scope: A percent is a rate per 100: 25% means 25 out of every 100. To find a percent of a number, find that part of the whole: 25% is one-fourth, 10% is one-tenth.
sourceSkills.misconception: A percent is not a count of things. 25% of 40 does not mean 25 things; it means one-fourth of 40, the size of one group when 40 is split into four equal groups.

prerequisites.title: Find a fraction of a whole

sourceSkills.title: Evaluate expressions
sourceSkills.scope: To evaluate an expression, replace each variable with its value and compute, following the order of operations: parentheses first, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction, left to right.
sourceSkills.misconception: Working strictly left to right gives the wrong value when a multiplication comes after an addition. Multiply before you add unless parentheses say otherwise.

sourceSkills.title: Solve one-step equations
sourceSkills.scope: An equation says two expressions are equal, like a balanced scale. To solve it, undo the operation on x by doing the inverse operation to BOTH sides, so the scale stays balanced.
sourceSkills.misconception: Doing the SAME operation that is in the equation (adding when it says + 4) moves x further away. Use the inverse operation, and do it to both sides.

sourceSkills.title: Absolute value and the coordinate plane
sourceSkills.scope: The absolute value of a number is its distance from 0, so it is never negative. On the coordinate plane, the signs of (x, y) tell which side of each axis a point is on, and distance to an axis is an absolute value.
sourceSkills.misconception: The axis you reflect across is the one that stays the same. Reflecting across the x-axis flips the point up or down, so only y changes sign.

sourceSkills.title: Find area of triangles and polygons
sourceSkills.scope: A triangle is exactly half of a parallelogram with the same base and height, so its area is A = ½ × base × height. The height is measured at a right angle to the base.
sourceSkills.misconception: base × height is the area of the whole parallelogram (or rectangle). The triangle is half of it.

sourceSkills.title: Divide multi-digit numbers
sourceSkills.scope: Long division shares a large number into equal groups one place value at a time: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down the next digit. Each digit of the quotient tells how many groups at that place.
sourceSkills.misconception: Skipping a 0 in the quotient makes it 10 times too small. Compare with your estimate: the number of digits should match.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The Grade 6 Studio's division skill works with fractions and decimals. This source set is whole-number long division.

sourceSkills.title: Order rational numbers
sourceSkills.scope: On a number line, numbers increase from left to right. A negative number with a larger absolute value is farther left, so it is LESS: −1 < −3/4.
sourceSkills.misconception: Ordering negatives by their size without the sign puts them backwards. −3/4 is closer to 0 than −1, so −3/4 is the greater number.

sourceSkills.title: Find the whole from a percent
sourceSkills.scope: When you know a part and the percent it is, you can find the whole. If 12 is 20% of a number, then 12 is one-fifth of it, so the whole is 5 groups of 12.
sourceSkills.misconception: The number you are given is the PART, not the whole. Taking a percent of it makes it smaller; the whole must be bigger than the part.

sourceSkills.title: Write equivalent expressions
sourceSkills.scope: Equivalent expressions have the same value for EVERY value of the variable. The distributive property, a(x + b) = ax + ab, multiplies every term inside the parentheses; factoring runs it backwards.
sourceSkills.misconception: The number outside the parentheses multiplies EVERY term inside, not only the first. Substitute a value for x to check that both expressions agree.

sourceSkills.title: Write and graph inequalities
sourceSkills.scope: An inequality describes ALL the values that make a condition true, not one value. “At least 58” includes 58 (≥, a closed dot); “more than 58” does not (>, an open dot).
sourceSkills.misconception: Check two things: the direction (greater or less) and whether the boundary itself is allowed (≥ ≤ include it, > < do not). Test a number to be sure.

sourceSkills.title: Dot plots, histograms and box plots
sourceSkills.scope: A data display organizes values so you can read them at a glance. A frequency table counts how many values fall in each category; a histogram counts how many fall in each equal interval.
sourceSkills.misconception: In a frequency table, the category (like “3 books”) is a label and the frequency is how many people. Add the frequencies to count the people.

sourceSkills.title: Mean, median, MAD and IQR
sourceSkills.scope: A measure of center (mean or median) gives one number to represent the data; a measure of spread (MAD or IQR) tells how far the values typically are from that center.
sourceSkills.misconception: The range uses the two extreme values; the IQR uses only the middle half. Order the data, find Q1 and Q3, then subtract.

sourceSkills.title: Surface area from nets
sourceSkills.scope: Surface area is the total area of all the faces of a solid. A net unfolds the solid flat, so you can find the area of each face and add them.
sourceSkills.misconception: length × width × height is the VOLUME, the space inside. Surface area covers the outside: add the areas of every face in the net.

sourceSkills.title: Volume with fractional edges
sourceSkills.scope: The volume of a rectangular prism is V = length × width × height, even when the edges are fractions. With ½-unit edges, the prism fills with small cubes that are each 1/8 of a unit cube.
sourceSkills.misconception: Multiplying only the whole numbers drops part of every edge. Change each mixed number to a fraction first, then multiply all three.

sourceSkills.title: Add and subtract integers
sourceSkills.scope: Adding a negative number moves you left on the number line; subtracting a negative moves you right. A positive chip and a negative chip make a zero pair, which is worth 0.
sourceSkills.misconception: Subtracting a negative is not the same as subtracting. a − (−b) means add the opposite: a + b.

sourceSkills.title: Multiply and divide integers
sourceSkills.scope: When you multiply or divide two integers, find the size from the absolute values and the sign from a rule: same signs give a positive result, different signs give a negative result.
sourceSkills.misconception: Two negatives make a positive in multiplication and division, not in addition. Decide the sign from the rule after you find the size.

sourceSkills.title: Operations with rational numbers
sourceSkills.scope: Signed fractions follow the same rules as integers, and fractions follow the same rules as always: add and subtract with a common denominator; multiply across; divide by multiplying by the reciprocal.
sourceSkills.misconception: Adding the numerators and adding the denominators does not add fractions: the pieces must be the same size first. Find a common denominator.

sourceSkills.title: Unit rates with decimals
sourceSkills.scope: A unit rate is the amount for exactly 1 unit. With decimals the reasoning is the same as with whole numbers: divide the total by the number of units.
sourceSkills.misconception: The amount for 1 item must be LESS than the total for several items. If your answer is bigger, you multiplied instead of dividing.

sourceSkills.title: Solve proportions
sourceSkills.scope: A proportion says two ratios are equivalent: a/b = x/c. Find the factor that turns one denominator into the other, and apply the SAME factor to the numerator.
sourceSkills.misconception: Ratios grow by multiplying, not by adding the same amount. Find what the denominator was multiplied by.

sourceSkills.title: Discounts and percent change
sourceSkills.scope: A percent change is a percent OF the original amount. Find that amount and add it for an increase or subtract it for a decrease, or multiply once: an increase of 25% gives 125% of the original.
sourceSkills.misconception: A percent is not a number of units. A 10% increase on 190 is not 190 + 10; find 10% of 190 first.

sourceSkills.title: Use scale drawings
sourceSkills.scope: A scale such as 1 cm : 5 m is a ratio between drawing lengths and real lengths. Every length in the drawing is multiplied by the same factor to give the real length.
sourceSkills.misconception: Adding the scale to the drawing length does not scale it. Multiply the drawing length by the real distance one unit stands for.

sourceSkills.title: Two-step equations
sourceSkills.scope: A two-step equation like 6x + 3 = 87 has two operations on x. Undo them in reverse order, doing the same thing to both sides each time: first remove the constant, then divide by the coefficient.
sourceSkills.misconception: An equation is a balance. Changing only one side breaks it: every step must be applied to BOTH sides.

sourceSkills.title: Test inequality solutions
sourceSkills.scope: A number is a solution of an inequality when it makes the statement true. Substitute the number, then compare using the number line: farther right is greater, even for negatives.
sourceSkills.misconception: Comparing negatives by their size without the sign reverses the answer. On the number line, the number farther right is greater.

sourceSkills.title: Circle area fluency
sourceSkills.scope: The area of a circle is A = πr²: the radius squared, times π. Cut a circle into thin slices and rearrange them; they form a shape close to a rectangle r tall and half the circumference (πr) long.
sourceSkills.misconception: 2r (the diameter) belongs to circumference, C = 2πr. Area squares the radius: r × r.

prerequisites.title: Find area of triangles and polygons

sourceSkills.title: Probability and measures of center
sourceSkills.scope: The probability of an event is (favorable outcomes) ÷ (all equally likely outcomes), a number from 0 to 1. The mean, median and range describe a data set's center and spread.
sourceSkills.misconception: P(win) compares the winning sections with ALL sections, not with the losing ones.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: The unsplit source generator mixes probability with measures of center. The Studio probability objective does not include measures of center.

sourceSkills.title: Combine like terms
sourceSkills.scope: Like terms have exactly the same variable part, such as 8x and −5x, or 6 and −4. Combining like terms adds their coefficients; each term keeps the sign in front of it.
sourceSkills.misconception: A minus sign belongs to the term right after it. In 8x + 6 − 5x − 4, the x-terms are 8x and −5x, and the constants are 6 and −4.

sourceSkills.title: Circumference of a circle
sourceSkills.scope: Every circle's circumference is a little more than 3 times its diameter; that ratio is π ≈ 3.14. So C = πd, and because d = 2r, also C = 2πr.
sourceSkills.misconception: Check which length you are given: C = π × d uses the diameter. With a radius, double it first (C = 2πr).

sourceSkills.title: Angle facts: lines and triangles
sourceSkills.scope: Angles that form a straight line add to 180°. When two lines cross, the angles directly across from each other (vertical angles) are equal. The three angles of any triangle add to 180°.
sourceSkills.misconception: A straight angle is 180°, not 90°. Use 90° only when the angles form a right angle.

sourceSkills.title: Predict from a random sample
sourceSkills.scope: A random sample is a smaller group chosen so every member of the population has the same chance of being picked. Its rate (like 24 out of 40) predicts the same rate in the whole population.
sourceSkills.misconception: Do not add the extra people to the count. The population has the same FRACTION as the sample, so multiply the population by the sample fraction.

sourceSkills.title: Evaluate integer exponents
sourceSkills.scope: An exponent tells how many times the base is used as a FACTOR: 3⁴ = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3. It is repeated multiplication, not multiplication by the exponent.
sourceSkills.misconception: 3⁴ is not 3 × 4. Write the base as a factor as many times as the exponent says, then multiply.

sourceSkills.title: Powers of ten
sourceSkills.scope: Multiplying by 10ⁿ moves every digit n places to the LEFT (the number gets larger); multiplying by 10⁻ⁿ, which is dividing by 10ⁿ, moves every digit n places to the right.
sourceSkills.misconception: A negative exponent makes the number SMALLER, not negative. 3.2 × 10⁻² = 0.032.

sourceSkills.title: Perfect square roots
sourceSkills.scope: The square root of n is the number that, multiplied by itself, gives n. Geometrically, √n is the side length of a square with area n.
sourceSkills.misconception: A square root is not half the number. √n times ITSELF must give n; check by multiplying.

sourceSkills.title: Solve linear equations
sourceSkills.scope: To solve a linear equation, isolate the variable by applying inverse operations to BOTH sides, in reverse order of operations. Each step produces an equivalent equation with the same solution.
sourceSkills.misconception: Every operation must happen on both sides. Dividing only the right side, or subtracting only on the left, changes the equation.

sourceSkills.title: Find slope from two points
sourceSkills.scope: Slope is the rate of change of a line: how much y changes for each 1-unit change in x. Between two points, slope = (change in y) ÷ (change in x) = (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁).
sourceSkills.misconception: Slope is rise over run: the change in y goes on TOP. Subtract the coordinates in the same order in the numerator and the denominator.

sourceSkills.title: Evaluate linear functions
sourceSkills.scope: A function assigns exactly one output to each input. For y = mx + b, multiply the input x by the rate m, then add the starting value b.
sourceSkills.misconception: A negative input keeps its sign when you substitute. Write it in parentheses, like 5(−3), so the sign is not lost.

sourceSkills.title: Solve simple systems
sourceSkills.scope: A system of two equations asks for the values that make BOTH true at once: the point where the two lines cross. Adding x + y = a and x − y = b eliminates y, because +y and −y cancel.
sourceSkills.misconception: After adding the equations you have 2x, not x: divide by 2. And make sure you report the variable that was asked for.

sourceSkills.title: Solve angle relationship problems
sourceSkills.scope: Complementary angles add to 90°, supplementary angles add to 180°, and vertical angles, across from each other where two lines cross, are equal.
sourceSkills.misconception: Complementary → 90°, supplementary → 180°. Memory aid: “C” comes before “S”, and 90 comes before 180.

sourceSkills.title: Pythagorean theorem
sourceSkills.scope: In a right triangle, the squares on the two legs together have the same area as the square on the hypotenuse: a² + b² = c². The hypotenuse is the side across from the right angle, and it is the longest side.
sourceSkills.misconception: c ≠ a + b. Square each leg, add the squares, and then take the square root.

sourceSkills.title: Identify bivariate association
sourceSkills.scope: Two quantities have a positive association when y tends to increase as x increases, a negative association when y tends to decrease, and no association when there is no overall trend.
sourceSkills.misconception: “Negative” describes the direction (y falls as x rises), not negative numbers. All the values can be positive in a negative association.

sourceSkills.title: Coordinate reflections (extension)
sourceSkills.scope: A reflection flips a figure over a line like a mirror. Across the x-axis, (x, y) → (x, −y); across the y-axis, (x, y) → (−x, y); through the origin, both signs change: (x, y) → (−x, −y).
sourceSkills.misconception: Reflecting across the x-axis changes y, not x: the point flips up or down over the horizontal axis.

sourceSkills.title: Operations with scientific notation
sourceSkills.scope: To multiply numbers in scientific notation, multiply the coefficients and ADD the exponents, because 10ᵃ × 10ᵇ = 10ᵃ⁺ᵇ. Then make sure the coefficient is at least 1 and less than 10.
sourceSkills.misconception: Exponents are added when powers of ten are MULTIPLIED, not multiplied. And when you ADD numbers with the same power, the power stays the same.

sourceSkills.title: Volume of cylinders, cones and spheres
sourceSkills.scope: A cylinder's volume is the base area times the height: V = πr²h. A cone with the same base and height holds exactly one-third as much, V = ⅓πr²h. A sphere's volume is V = (4/3)πr³.
sourceSkills.misconception: The radius is SQUARED in the base area (r × r), not doubled; and the cone needs the ⅓.
sourceSkills.catalogOnlyReason: Grade 8 Studio lacks a volume objective. Its closest geometry desk covers transformations and similarity.

sourceSkills.title: Translations, rotations and dilations
sourceSkills.scope: A translation slides every point the same distance and direction: (x, y) → (x + a, y + b). A rotation turns points about the origin: 90° counterclockwise gives (−y, x) and 180° gives (−x, −y). A dilation by k from the origin gives (kx, ky).
sourceSkills.misconception: A 180° rotation changes BOTH signs; changing one sign is a reflection. Sketch the point and its image to check.

sourceSkills.title: Compare two functions
sourceSkills.scope: The rate of change of a linear function is its slope: how much y changes for each 1 that x increases. Functions can be given as equations, tables, graphs or words; find the rate in each form before comparing.
sourceSkills.misconception: The y-intercept is where a line starts, not how fast it changes. Compare the rates (slopes), not the starting values.

destinationSkills.title: Strategies: make ten and doubles

fluency.rationale: Find the amount that makes ten.
